review:
After around 100 hours in Blue Protocol, I have several thoughts that I feel need to be considered. This game is trying to strike a balance between popular MMOs like WoW, FF14, GW2, and ESO and, most notably, the Hoyoverse games. In some ways I do think that it succeeds in making a "Hoyoverse MMO", but in other ways, it has a lot to improve. 

Graphics Quality: 8/10. I think that the quality is good, though there are some instances even on high graphics where NPCs' teeth don't load in during cutscenes and such.

Sound/Music Quality: 7/10. Like the graphics, I think the quality is perfectly fine, though I do think that the generic battle theme is highly repetitive and could have been a bit less of something that I'd rather mute and play my own music over after several hours.

Story: 3/10. Way too fast-paced. I won't go into spoilers, but the story for this game moves at 100 miles an hour, to the point that most "important" character moments for the cast of NPCs fall flat because we've only known them for five minutes. I think that the developers focused way too hard on having a story that they could reasonably deliver during the opening hype for the game. If you didn't keep up the story with the small daily chunks they timegated off during the first two weeks of the game, I think a playthrough of the first arc could maybe be only 6 hours long, with you only being familiar with the main villain for 1.5-2 hours of that. The characters also, in medias res, act like major things have happened in-universe in the span of you doing a 2 minute puzzle. I genuinely wonder if there were plans for there to be like 30-50% more quest content and they just cut it for some reason or another. 

Localization: Tied to story. My GOD the locatlization in this game is ROUGH. Most of the localization is fine, if not a little awkward, but some of them are just atrocious. I think one of the text boxes I found with placeholder "Type Here" text just said "Please". PLEASE have someone go over the text before it gets shipped.

Quality Assurance: 6/10. Not great. I learned that apparently dialogue in the game is built in HTML since I noticed one of the lines of dialogue had a ? instead of a > to line break. Some sentences are missing spaces between words, it's not uncommon to randomly disconnect at times, and I noticed a sound bug in one of the high-level areas where the sound randomly starts and stops. This game REALLY needed another month or two of QA testing before release.

Class Design: 9/10. I actually really like the classes in this game and look forward to any future releases they may put out. While most of them have clear analogues to other MMOs (Frost Mage being WoW frost mage, Wind Knight being FFXIV Dragoon, etc.), I don't think that's a bad thing. They're aesthetics that people are familiar with and already like. Also, THIS GAME GIVES YOU TIPS AND USE CASES FOR YOUR INDIVIDUAL CLASS ABILITIES! How have the other big MMOs not done this yet? Massive props from me.

Fight Design: 9/10. The Master difficulty fights aren't out yet, but I've been pleasantly surprised with what I've seen so far in the "casual" content. AoE dodges, add phases, rot passes from FFXIV, and more. If the high-end combat was more accessible to the average player, I'd give this a 10/10. 

Economy: 2/10. Garbage-tier. There are approximately 8 different currencies to keep track of, each with their own weekly/monthly lockouts, and two of them are just "unbound/f2p" versions, with one being presented as the "general currency" and the other being the "freemium". Ironically, for the purposes that you need them for, the "general currency" feels like the most you want and is harder to obtain in meaningful amounts. In other MMOs, you'd just supplement this by using crafting and gathering to make things to sell and vendor mob drops. THERE IS NO VENDOR TO SELL SURPLUS MOB DROPS. YOU WILL BE STUCK WITH THEM FOREVER. I'll get into crafting and gathering next, but the game systems have essentially culminated in the classes needing massive amounts of the "general currency" to progress your character, but not having enough to actually do anything for it. This is probably my biggest complaint in the entire game aside from the crafting and gathering.

Crafting / Gathering: 1/10. This game has a stamina system for crafting and gathering. It's shared between all of the "life skills", so you have to pick and choose what you want to do every day. If you don't use stamina, you gain 1/40 of the exp you would have if you used stamina. This is honestly just not acceptable. Other MMOs have tried to do this and it hasn't really worked out. This needs to not be a thing. What happens if you have a raid group that needs food and "serums", but you're capped on your stamina or don't have enough to make what you need? It's bad enough trying to level one of them, but there's around 8 life skills in total. If you're like me and like having one of every crafter and gatherer in MMOs, this is going to be a LONG grind for you.

Fashion: 4/10. I like making my characters look good in MMOs. I like DOING CONTENT that lets me get things that make my characters look good in MMOs. 99% of the fashion choices in this game are paid. I do like what's on offer, but I'm not inclined to spend upwards of $10 for an outfit in this game for the sake of just not being in the default outfit.

I don't know how the CN players reacted to a lot of the problems in the game, particularly since localization presumably wasn't much of a thing that they had to consider, but I genuinely wonder why the developers thought some of these decisions were acceptable. That being said, the F2P in this game is quite reasonable, I'd just have much rather paid to buy this game than deal with the stamina and currency woes. Otherwise though, great game. I'd recommend for at least something to enjoy yourself in, but the developers have made it hard to consider this as a "daily driver".

My main recommendations for improvement are: Remove the stamina system from crafting and gathering so the player economy can start to grow instead of whatever it's doing now. Open up vendors so players can sell mob drops to make some pocket change or at least exchange them for something usable. Condense the 8 different currencies - or at least just merge the bound and unbound ones. Spend more time proofreading the lines of dialogue in the game. Spend some time crafting a story rather than drip-feeding it and acting like major things have been happening. I want to like this game and I will play for the foreseeable future, but if this game wants to survive long-term, there are changes that need to happen.

22/05/2026 - The game's publisher has recently demonstrated serious incompetence in handling major issues within the game.

The day before this edit, all players received [url=https://i.imgur.com/Es6Jvms.png]an in-game mail containing roughly $100 worth of premium currency, with the message clearly indicating it was a gift[/url]. As a result, many players who reasonably assumed this was a legitimate gift have effectively ended up with over $100 worth of negative premium currency (which, mind you, can only normally be obtained through real-money purchases).

Choosing this approach instead of issuing a rollback, especially given how little time had passed, is baffling from every angle. It also remains unclear whether carrying a premium currency debt may eventually result in account bans.

Day 1 player here.

I really wanted to enjoy this game. I genuinely tried to put aside the initial negative reviews and my own doubts, just to give it a fair shot and find something to like.

That lasted until around the middle of Season 2.

Once you’ve seen one season, you’ve basically seen them all. The loop is predictable: new gear drops that immediately invalidate whatever you’ve been working toward, seasonal activities that feel designed more to keep the game open than to be engaging, the same structure of three raid bosses across difficulties, and a handful of dungeons recycling rewards with slight variations.

On top of that, there’s a constant stat crunch, new paid “summons” that overshadow older ones, and more fashion sets locked behind an overpriced gacha system.

At its core, it’s a gacha game that doesn’t respect your time or your investment.

It tries to appeal to hardcore MMO grinders, but the systems are too shallow to support that, while simultaneously being too demanding for a more casual audience. It ends up stuck in an awkward middle ground where neither playstyle feels satisfying.

Even the one strong point I initially enjoyed the game for, fashion, is starting to feel stale. Recent additions lean heavily into repetitive, cutesy designs, with little variety or creativity, and the male options in particular feel like like they were created with random additions and seeing what sticks.

It’s just not worth the time commitment, and definitely not worth the money. Both feel wasted here. Stay away.

I think after almost 80 hours... I'm good. 

I really wanted to love this game. I spent so long waiting for it. I was heartbroken when I saw the original game was shut down. Was ecstatic to hear it was coming back, in one form or another. I played it for all this time, joined a guild with nice people, even spent money to pick up an outfit or two. But I don't know, this game makes you feel kind of empty.

When such-and-such character dies, it's kind of sudden and there was no real attachment there because we only knew them for maybe 3-4 quests, and I found myself not feeling anything particular about it even though it was treated as something super sad for the other characters. I think that was probably the first moment I started wondering if I was actually enjoying the story. Cutscenes are incredibly cheaply made, sometimes they're just slideshows with blurbs of text in between, or sometimes they're just 5 seconds of a character turning to look your way. Dialogue is okay if you engage in it, but there's no incentive to, and you'll reach the same end every time.

Movement speed is incredibly slow, even on a mount. It's hard playing this game and swapping back to one that's faster paced. Your character sprints at full tilt, but it never really seems like you're going anywhere. Thankfully there's auto navigation for most content, so you can do something else while your character travels to wherever you pointed to.

Combat's... okay, but I stopped bothering to watch my cooldowns and use skills myself and opted to just use the auto-combat after a while. Fighting started feeling like a chore. Boss fights are fine though, it wasn't hard to understand mechanics, and if you played with bot teammates, they'd handle most of the mechanics themselves, leaving you to focus on dealing damage.

Other reviews have already mentioned how the cash shop currency doesn't carry over between your 3 characters, nor does any other purchase you make. It was a little jarring finding that out AFTER buying an outfit.

The daily loop was probably the most draining part about the game. It's all about grinding and gearing and busting your butt thinking you've finally earned all the best gear-- right before an update invalidates it all by adding in a tier higher. I get that it's a "Welcome to MMO's" moment and I shouldn't be surprised by it, but the amount of work you had to put to get fully geared was A Lot. Add to that daily/weekly limits and you'll almost always end up behind somehow. Log in, do a boss fight or two, do your guild dailies, log out. It's easy to burn out unless you've got people you're playing with doing it with you.

While I appreciate that the game came back at all, it just feels soul-crushingly average at best.

Okay, I like waiting to review games to give them a fair review & not make rash judgements based on superficial whims.  With that said, and nearly 500 hours clocked into this game I cannot in good faith recommend this game. I *really* wanted to give a positive review as well. 

The game is p2w, what you win: superiority and bragging rights of being top dps, if you pick the right class. Sink time and money into the wrong class and you’ll be just above average. 

The gatekeeping and community is 90% of what killed the player base. People treated this like a hardcore MMO, when the reality is you have 5 buttons, a few basic PvE mechanics that are nothing new, and relies on team work. People in world chats upset that they can’t find groups to clear content a week old being met with “uninstall” “baby’s first MMO”. 

There is an “auto battle” feature, which is awesome as you can toggle skills to be on auto or not. Really great for stuff that you constantly have in rotation that needs to be used the moment it’s off CD. The auto battle does not “battle” it just activates skills, and even times certain spells to maximise dps. Great feature for when there’s a lot of movement or aoe happening, however that of course is a problem. Many players call for “auto battle banned in dungeons and raids” “will be kicked if on auto”. 

The lack of content. When the game first released, this was not a problem what so ever as there was a *ton* of stuff unlocking so no biggie that the story is time gated, no worries that life skills have a cap. However, now that the game is towards the end of the season there’s no more random chests scattered around as they’ve been found, there’s no more books to find, there’s no more maps unlocking, you can’t grind you skills because limited stamina, all content is reclears, helping others. 

There’s literally nothing to do if you’ve been playing since day 1 and clearing content semi casually each week. Further more exacerbated by p2w carrying entire parties and making what should take an hour or so a 5 minute raid or dungeon. Everyone just leaves parties as quickly as possible. 

The social aspect of the game is abysmal. There’s no way to chat locally and have it make sense, if you’re in a map, then the “current” channel is for the entire map, not local to a current radius. There’s no social hang outs, no idle games or events, literally nothing that helps players connect beyond guilds. 

I was a guild leader, had tons of quality players, good personalities, smart people, engaging with building a good community. Was awesome the first couple weeks, then the drop offs started happening, no problem recruited more players, then they fell off. Okay, recruit more players, okay now maybe recruit lagging guilds… and the cycle never stops as there are literally thousands of players each week who fall off. 

I never struggled to find a group, knew how to ask in world chat for groups, make friends, find players. That was never an issue. There are dozens of players I know who quit because they didn’t put in that effort, and it was difficult to get parties together, would take me a good 10-15m sometimes for dungeons, 30 or so minutes for raids. 

The “dailies” are an absolute joke. You can buy over priced items from a mystery shop, you must buy the battle pass to get an extra refresh, and the item pricing doesn’t even make sense, it’s completely random. Sometimes you’ll find stamina potions for 100 orbs, or you’ll find them for 10,000 luno. 

There’s 10+ currencies in game, half expire at the end of the season, they don’t roll over and they don’t tell you which ones expire. 

I didn’t mind any of these glaring flaws because my friends were playing and we were all having fun. The fun is now now feels like a daily grind / chores, almost all my friends have stopped playing, in game and the ones out of the game. 

I was holding out for season 2 but have read multiple sources saying there will be p2w weapons and items that further the dps gaps, AND 0 balance changes. This info was the nail in coffin for me. 

Cannot recommend this game, sadly. I stuck through the bugs, I dealt with the drops offs, I “made my own community”, I cleared content at a normal pace. Now that the newness has worn off, this game is literally just click some items, clear ez mode dungeons, teleport to a location, afk farm.

I put over 400 hours into Blue Protocol: Star Resonance, so I definitely got my money's worth in terms of playtime. I enjoyed the game for a while, but I can't honestly recommend it to anyone looking for an MMO they can invest in long-term.

Let's start with the positives. The visuals are excellent. The anime art style is beautiful, and the character creator gives you plenty of options to make a character that feels unique. Fashion is also one of the game's biggest draws—but it comes with a major caveat. While there are a lot of great cosmetics, many of the best outfits are locked behind limited-time gacha banners. On top of that, the dye system is surprisingly restrictive. Several outfits, including collaborations like Monogatari and Fairy Tail, don't let you freely recolor every part of the costume, which makes customization feel far more limited than it should.

Unfortunately, that's where most of my praise ends.

The story is incredibly forgettable. It mostly feels like you're moving from one area to the next without much reason to care about what's happening.

The biggest issue is the endgame. Once you reach it, you realize just how shallow the gameplay loop really is. Every day becomes the same routine: gather and craft until you run out of stamina, either stop playing or burn potions to keep gathering, run your daily boss run (Unstable fights which take around 20 seconds with an AI party), and farm bosses hoping for imagines drops so you can play. I spent 6 months doing the same boss everyday and only had 1 imagine drop. ( Don't even bother tanking unless you have Tempest Ogre. He feels mandatory)

That's... pretty much it.

There are weekly raids, but unless you're in an active guild, you'll either struggle to find a group or hope you get lucky with a decent PUG. Progression is also frustrating because many groups refuse to accept players unless they already have an absurdly high Ability Score. It's a classic case gatekeeping.

I joined a few guilds that simply carried me through the harder content. While I appreciated the help, it also made progression feel hollow because I wasn't really earning anything.

The dungeon design doesn't help either. Most seasons simply recycle the same few dungeons across three different difficulty levels. New dungeons are added each season, but they usually boil down to pulling as many enemies as possible, AoEing everything down, and then fighting a boss.

Seasonal events aren't much better. Most are either AFK events or small minigames that lose their appeal after a handful of runs.

Eventually, I realized I was logging in every single day just to complete my dailies without actually having fun. Then the next season would arrive, wipe most of my progression, and send me back to square one. Instead of feeling rewarded for my time, it felt like I was on a treadmill that never went anywhere.

I haven't logged in for a few weeks now, and honestly, it's been a relief. I don't miss the daily checklist.

This game has a fantastic foundation. The visuals, character customization, and overall presentation are genuinely good. But the repetitive endgame, seasonal resets, shallow progression, restrictive cosmetic systems, and overreliance on limited-time gacha keep it from reaching its potential.

 I don't regret the time I spent with it, but I can't recommend it unless you're simply looking for a casual anime MMO to play for a season or two without expecting much depth.

It’s a shame that this is how it ended, because the game actually had a lot of potential. The management made a long series of bad decisions and ended up ruining it. The game had a lovingly crafted world, great enemies, interesting raids, cute costumes, and in the beginning even the monetization felt acceptable.

I was there from day one, I had a great guild, made Friends, but the game became uninteresting to me very quickly because of the timegating. It clearly wanted to be accessible and make it easy for players to jump back in, even if they had missed a week. But what it actually achieved was punishing active players. Someone who logged in once a week could get the same gear in half an hour as a player who had invested several hours every day.

Even raid rewards that were supposed to be difficult to earn were basically handed out to everyone at the end of the week, regardless of whether they had even attempted the raid. Because of the heavy timegating, you quickly ran out of things to do, and the only remaining goal became the seasonal costumes from dungeons. But since there was no pity system at all, you could grind a dungeon over 100 times and still never get the skin you wanted.

Progress was so heavily restricted that within just a few weeks, you could complete nearly every achievement, and in the end fishing and gathering became the only things left to do. But since botting was not punished, even there a player who left a fishing bot running for a few nights was far ahead of a normal active player.

And now there’s apparently even going to be a button that boosts you straight to level 60. They wanted to attract casual players, but instead they drove away the active player base. What came out of it is a dead game that could have been a truly great experience otherwise.

It doesn't seem to have a core identity for me. If you are a more hardcore, dedicated player, the game feels really small and repetitive, effort seems not to be rewarded in this. Classes are unbalanced, progression feel pointless as the cap is raised too fast/often and requires no effort, very few cosmetics for f2p players, only 3 free pulls a week on the gacha banner.

If you are a casual player there doesn't seem to have much about this game. Because like I said, things require barely any effort. The social aspect is good, as guilds seem to a nice opportunity to meet friends, but everything nowadays is Discord and you are barely required to do any activity in a group honestly maybe just a few raids but there are alternate options to get the same gear (buy tokens from the weekly shop).

This is the shortened version of the review as the original one was over the character review limit by 6.5K characters. The review mainly talked about the bad points of the game

TLDR: The game prioritizes a good short term experience, where they make the player spend as much on the game as possible

At the time of writing, the current season is 3 (S3). Everything is subject to change (and let's hope it will (for the better))

This is what you'll be greeted by when you start (assuming you start at the beginning of a season): The main story quest which you don't have to engage with at all (despite being an MMORPG). The devs worked very hard to make it just an MMO. You'll see that your character is already at the max level because they wanted to make newbies be able to catch up to the latest content as quick as possible. The next thing you'll notice is a friend request from Maria, an infamous bot account made for scamming people. Yes, people do complain about the bot problem in the official discord server and yet, they don't get banned. Now, you take a glance at the world chat where you'll see players discussing how nice the newly implemented QoL features are (that they could've implemented anytime but decided to wait until the start of the next season.) Some of them should've been there since the start of the game and others make you wonder whether they made some parts of the game bad on purpose just so they could later fix it like this

The game wants to make the initial impression as nice as possible and get new players up to speed. There's a special store that let's you buy all the rewards you would've got from content you missed. The currency for it is earned by just playing the game normally. Any items from the previous season become obsolete. Do you remember Maria, whom you've probably blocked? You should have gotten another friend request from them by now, which is your first encounter with the broken features and the lack of basic QA testing this game has to offer

You get non-raid gear from dungeons. You'll quickly come to hate them as you'll have to grind these a lot to get the gear you want. So far, each season added QoL fixes to make them more bearable
S2: guaranteed gold gear
S3: you'll only get gear for a the class you select
You only need gold gear from almost right off the bat
Some dungeons from S1 got reused in S3 with barely any changes made to them

There are other ways to acquire gear
craft them, but crafted gear is way worse
raids (these get you raid gear, which is what you'll be using)

When it comes to gear, you only need to care about the illusion breaking strength stat, which I'll be calling ILSTR. Anything besides that is just optimization. If you have less of it than your enemy then you'll deal greatly reduced damage and receive significantly more damage. Having more has less impact

Next, you'll want to upgrade your gear. There's 3 kinds of upgrades
Reforging; you'll quickly notice that you have a limited amount of the items needed for reforging and there's not a lot of ways to get them. You can buy them from the trading center or wait for the weekly refresh
Refining (expensive, obsolete, no ILSTR): you upgrade the gear slots. Can fail; you can use items to boost your chances of success
Embedding: Became worse rather than better over time. You used to embed gems to your gear until you hit the major stat boost that you have a 5% chance to get. Now, you embed sigils. These are random boss drops which you can only get by using your keys (you get 2 a day and can carry up to 6 at a time.) You still have to craft gems to embed those sigils

Crafting upgrade materials require you to use focus (AKA stamina; you get 400 a day and can store up to 2000) and materials you have to gather using focus. Even better, the amount of materials you get are random
Gathering and crafting involves a lot of RNG for the amount of items received and for the level of the potions and foods

By design, the game makes sure that you cannot get enough materials at a decent pace; and that's where the trading center comes in. You can buy and sell unbound materials for unbound Luno. You can also buy the the moss mech shard, which cannot be crafted (but is still listed under the life skills -> smithing category). And then there's the materials for the "whale weapon" that becomes obsolete by the time you can acquire it without buying the materials from here

There are 2 more subsystems for character progression
Modules (the gear that is technically not gear): the upgrade button has been unimplemented since S1, RNG, limited amount, buy more from the trading center
Imagines (summons):  get will and other materials to craft & upgrade them (low drop rate from bosses and you need keys for it) or buy them from the trading center or the gacha or from the guild hunt. You can also get them from stimens vault (the most hated game mode. so much so, that one of the QoL features that they've added is that you don't have to start from the very first floor after the reset)

You can buy/sell unbound items for unbound Luno (the normal currency). The only exception to this are rose orbs (the premium currency.) When you buy rose orbs, they become bound items for a greedy reason

You can it now, can't you? You buy rose orbs for real money, sell them to get unbound Luno and buy any materials you need to get stronger. bound roser orbs are used for the will gacha and some items in the store. Unbound rose orbs used for the outfit gacha. Customization is the only decent feature this game, so you bet they'll monetize the heck out of it. This is why you cannot get unbound rose orbs from the trading center. You can buy 3 pulls a week for bound rose orbs as well, which is nowhere near enough. You can buy gacha outfits and mounts from the trading center for a lot of unbound Luno

Now let's talk about the gameplay.
The good parts: the MMO aspect (guilds, chatting and friend system); the customization (character and homestead) (no edits needed for this part)

And with those out of the way, back to talking about the majority of the game
* Raids: lot's of full party wipe mechanics and DPS checks. The former wouldn't be that bad if people were willing to learn the mechanics
* Poorly explained mechanics: The game does its absolute worst to properly explain raid and dungeon mechanics, you need a 3rd-party site to get a decent explanation
* Almost every feature has a bug
* CN/Global: the CN is way ahead. Despite that, the collaboration events happen at the same time. Both servers receive the same content, balanced for CN. Currently, they are trying to sync global up to CN, which includes giving us lots of valuable materials, so they locked those behind challenging gameplay
* Main story: It's being neglected (and it is pretty meh to begin with)
* Some of the maps are a bit too alike: we have a lot of maps that are just a big dense forest so I hope you like them
* For most classes, the skill tree has only one optimal build
* Class balancing is bad and there are classes that are barely played but I don't know the details

And for the finale, an example just how they only care about squeezing money out of the players: Once, every player received a gift from the mail that contained unbound rose orbs. This was unintentional as they quickly locked the mail feature so players cannot claim it and removed it from the inventory of those who already have

Apart from that, the only time they ever quickly fixed a bug is when it involved enabling the players to get more materials for outfit customization than intended. They removed either the excess items or the amount of rose orbs they are worth from the inventories of the players

And the worst part is, if you find a good guild, you can enjoy the MMO aspect of the game enough to keep playing

review:
Beautiful presentation, hollow endgame, this one nails the classic gacha-MMO trap of looking incredible on the surface while the actual loop underneath wears thin fast.

Pros
✔ Visuals are genuinely excellent, the anime art style is polished and the character creator gives real room to make something unique.
✔ Fashion and cosmetics are a major draw, with a wide variety of outfits and collab content like Monogatari and Fairy Tail.
✔ Strong initial presentation makes the first stretch of the game genuinely enjoyable for casual players.
✔ Good as a seasonal, low commitment anime MMO if you're not expecting long term depth.

Cons
✘ The dye system is surprisingly restrictive, several collab outfits don't allow full recoloring, undercutting the customization the game is otherwise praised for.
✘ Story is largely forgettable, more about moving between zones than giving you a reason to care.
✘ Endgame loop is shallow and repetitive, the same daily gather, craft, and boss run routine with minimal variation.
✘ Progression heavily gatekept by Ability Score requirements in group content, making it hard to advance without already being carried.
✘ Dungeon design recycles the same handful of layouts across difficulty tiers rather than offering real variety.
✘ Seasonal resets wipe progress and restart the grind, turning what should feel rewarding into a treadmill.
✘ Best cosmetics are locked behind limited-time gacha banners, adding a monetization layer on top of an already repetitive structure.

Overall
Blue Protocol: Star Resonance has a genuinely strong foundation, gorgeous presentation, solid character customization, and an inviting first impression. But the endgame doesn't hold up, seasonal resets undercut long-term investment, and progression leans too heavily on gatekeeping and gacha luck. Worth trying for a season if you want something casual and pretty, not worth committing to as a long-term MMO.

[*]The devs list items in the trading store themselves, and some of them you can't get anywhere else in the game. So it's not really a player market, it's a shop that rewards people who spend.
[*]Refinement is the old enhancement system with a % chance to fail. When it fails you lose the materials and get a 2% better chance next time. Some of the materials that lower the fail chance only come from those dev listings, you can't craft them and no player can sell them.
[*]You can buy skills, will materials and unbound luno with paid currency, so anyone with a credit card can just skip months of grinding.
[*]There are more than 20 currencies. You can properly farm maybe 3 or 4 of them. A few of the ones you need for your character are basically paid only.
[*]Free players can't really trade with each other because of the bound/unbound split. Only stuff made with Focus or bought with money can be traded.
[*]The mounts that look good cost hundreds of dollars, and the seasonal leaderboards are literally for who bought the most cosmetics.
[/list]

[h2]Progression is RNG on top of RNG[/h2]

Everything is time gated. You finish what there is to do, then you wait for the next gate, and then you wait again.

To craft a boss will you need the drop from the boss plus 15 crafting materials, nobody knows the drop rates, and you only get 2 keys a day. The best part is that the materials don't drop from the same boss, so you have to burn your keys on a different one.

More than 90% of the purple battle images and materials are useless. Gold replaces all of it and you can't even sell the purple stuff because nobody wants it. Gold modules can roll three healing stats when you're a DPS, and if you scrap one you get back about a quarter of a new one.

Then every new season brings some new power mechanic that makes the gear you spent hundreds of hours on worthless, and you start over.

The season gimmick itself is just leaving your game running AFK for hours to farm mob drops. The raids don't even use it. It's there to inflate playtime numbers and your AS. And because AS is the only thing people can look at, groups ask for ridiculous numbers for content you can clear with much less. A simple clear counter per boss would fix that, but nobody can sell you a clear counter.

[h2]Endgame and dailies[/h2]

The endgame is the same few raid fights on different difficulties, and the same dungeons from release with more HP and more damage.

Dailies feel like chores. The chests have a chance of giving you nothing useful, gold materials drop at single digit %, and boss wills at less than 1%. Commissions are the worst I've seen in any game, the same boring minigames over and over for bound luno you can't even use in the trading center.

Events are either standing AFK somewhere for 30 minutes or logging in to claim something. The story is go here, talk to this person, screen goes black, and a text tells you what happened instead of showing it.

[h2]Professions[/h2]

Everything that matters is locked behind Focus. A recipe that costs Focus gives 80 XP, one that doesn't gives 2 XP, and going from 1 to 50 takes 163k XP. And after all that, the gold gear you craft is much worse than dropped gear because it's missing a whole stat buff.

[h2]Players and servers[/h2]

There aren't enough people left for the dungeon queues. On master difficulty you wait 10 minutes or more and some queues never pop. The game wants you to fill the group with AI teammates, but the bots can't do the wipe mechanics, so the higher master dungeons are impossible with them.

They also cut the number of map lines by a lot, which made farming elites and bosses nearly impossible.

If you're not in NA you play with constant lag and dropped inputs. When the EU server finally came, there was no account migration. They expected people who played for a year to start from zero just to have decent ping, so obviously it was dead from the first day. Regions are locked too, so a playerbase that was already shrinking got split in half.

[h2]UI, chat and bugs[/h2]

[list]
[*]Only one chat channel can be fully customized. MMOs had custom chat tabs 20 years ago.
[*]The chat filter is so strict you can't even type the names of items that are in the game.
[*]The UI is a mess, with several different shop tabs, two season pass tabs and two gacha tabs.
[*]World chat is full of bots and script sellers all day and nobody bans them. Meanwhile the anti-cheat mostly just keeps non-Windows players out.
[/list]

[h2]How the devs treat players[/h2]

They sent premium rose orbs to everyone by mistake. When they noticed, the servers went down for emergency maintenance faster than they've ever reacted to an actual game-breaking bug. Then instead of doing a rollback, they took the orbs back from people who had already spent them and left those accounts with a negative balance that has to be paid off before buying anything else. No explanation and no apology.

I was a little bit debating about this review of mine, but here it is. Please, take into consideration that I am a female player and I see things -also- under this view.

⭐ Pros

1. Beautiful anime visuals.
The art direction is really good. Characters look expressive and vibrant, and the world feels like an interactive anime. If you enjoy that aesthetic, the game is a treat.

2. Smooth, responsive combat.
The combat is fast, stylish, and satisfying. Dodging, timing, and chaining abilities feels fluid. Boss fights are especially fun & flashy, challenging, and rewarding.

3. Good character customization.
As a female player, I appreciated the variety of hairstyles, outfits, and accessories. The game lets you build a character who actually feels like you instead of locking options behind gender stereotypes.

4. Social features and co-op feels natural.
Grouping up never feels forced. The game is designed for quick cooperation without awkward pressure. There is a nice balance between solo freedom and shared moments. If you join an active guild, that's even better. I was lucky.

5. Epic soundtrack.
The music is cinematic and uplifting, especially during story beats and big encounters.


❌ Cons

1.Heavy grinding.
A lot of progression is locked behind repetitive tasks. If you don’t enjoy farming materials or repeating the same dungeons, the game can feel exhausting.

2. Story pacing is inconsistent
Some story chapters are emotional and engaging, but others drag on or feel thin. The narrative sometimes struggles to hold the same level of excitement that the visuals promise.

3. Monetization needs polish.
While the game isn’t fully pay-to-win, cosmetics and convenience items are very obviously pushed. It occasionally breaks immersion when the shop feels more polished than the quest system.

4. Limited variety in enemy types.
Many enemies feel similar despite the different zones. The world is beautiful, but the mobs don’t always match that level of creativity.

5. Performance issues on certain devices.
Even with good hardware, the game sometimes stutters in crowded areas or large battles. Optimization still has room to grow.

Final Thoughts

Blue Protocol: Star Resonance is a beautiful and charming MMO with satisfying combat and a strong visual identity. As a female player, I loved the customization, the expressive characters, and the sense of adventure. However, the game still leans too hard on grinding, has unstable pacing, and shows some rough edges in monetization and performance.

If you love anime aesthetics and action-combat MMOs, you will enjoy it.
If you want rich storytelling or deep variety, you might find it lacking.

I played on the original server which only launched in Japan (you needed a Bandai Namco account with a VPN set to Japan) and I feel like this launch was pretty much a straight miss in the sense that it didn't accomplish what I think it could have. The gameplay feels very slow, questing is long and drawn out, some scenes are unskippable, and there are time limits on resources that limit gathering and crafting. The character customization is really not what I want out of a gacha, as there are so many random items that I would never put on my avatar and I rarely see others using them on their characters either. There are like 7 outfits that you can choose if you don't pay, and it just isn't a model that makes me want to spend money on it. It feels totally pointless and lame to play this game, so I don't recommend it.

review:
Blue Protocol: Star Resonance is a by-the-numbers anime MMO that doesn't do anything special to stand out. One of the game’s biggest highlights is the art style; it offers strong anime visuals, a colorful world, stylish characters, and pretty detailed environments. It also offers almost all of the MMO activities you'd expect: some world exploration, fighting world bosses, crafting, fishing, and dungeons/raids. The combat is also ok-ish, but nothing to write home about; it's action-oriented, and you get a handful of skills for each class.

But everything else about BP:SR is really dull and uninspired. The story is the most generic and clichéd stuff you can think about and puts you to sleep real fast (there's an option to skip most dialogue and cutscenes, but reading any of the interactions is really tiresome - I've only completed the first 3 chapters of season 1, but it was more than enough to convience me that the game is garbage); all cutscenes look stilted and robotic, and the mouth animations are not synced to the dialogue; the story pacing is all over the place, and story beats feel hastily put together; activities around the world are just filler and feel repetitive fast; the world traversal is abysmal, it's slow and sluggish and none of the 3 mounts I got for free or any of the traversal skills available made it any more fun; controls in general (walking/traversal and combat) feel unresponsive and there's always a delay to all your actions; the camera sometimes feels broken and you can't move it easily enough to see the world around you. Also, there's an instant level 60 boost for new players, which I found weird, but at least you can still progress through the initial story if you are so inclined. Plus, like in any Asian MMO, there are a billion different menus that you must open 1 at a time and collect every single reward manually (or at least I didn't find a Collect All button). The performance isn't great; I had FPS dips at times for no reason, and the game sometimes crashed after leaving it idle for 15-20 minutes. It also has a season pass (free and paid), a monthly subscription pass, and a cash shop. There are also multiple currencies, some of which I don't even know what they are used for and just make the game more confusing. I personally can't say if the game's P2W, as I got bored before reaching end-game, but from what I've read online, it's a very gacha-heavy MMO and feels more like a mobile MMO (the interface is also very ugly and very mobile-ish, and the UX is not great at all). On top of everything, there's also apparently time-gated content, which just feels like another nail in the coffin.

Overall, BP:SR makes a very bad first impression, and it doesn't do anything to make your stay in the world more fun. Actually, I feel like the more you play, the worse it gets.

review:
[b]I really wanted to give this game a chance.[/b]
I’ve wanted to play Blue Protocol (the original) ever since the first trailer dropped. I even played the Japanese version because I was so excited about it, and I was heartbroken when it was announced that it would be shut down.

Then Star Resonance was announced. I followed everything closely and tried to stay up to date with all the information. However, I feel that streamers who played the CN Beta and CN version gave us too much hope — or rather, too much cope — for this game.

[b]Here is my honest positive and negative feedback:[/b]

[h3]Positive Feedback[/h3]

[b]The world feels great.[/b]
The larger map in the first area (compared to the original Blue Protocol) feels exciting to explore, and the new additions are genuinely good improvements.

[b]New class: Verdant Oracle.[/b]
This is something I would have loved to see in the original Blue Protocol. It’s a full healer class with a great design and enjoyable skills.

[b]Movement and traversal.[/b]
The jumping and flying mechanics are fantastic. They make exploring the world fun and add a lot of freedom to movement.

[b]Color wheel customization.[/b]
Having a color wheel for character creation, clothing, and more is a great improvement over the old system.

[b]Social aspects.[/b]
The guild system and in-game social activities are well done, and they genuinely encourage interaction between players.

[h3]Negative Feedback[/h3]

[b]Character creation.[/b]
The character creation options were heavily reduced compared to the original. While a few new hairstyles were added, many features were removed. I would honestly prefer losing the color wheel if it meant bringing back the more varied body sizes. Also, the original version included “voice choices,” which are missing here.

[b]Megaserver issues.[/b]
If you want to run a megaserver for EU/NA and other regions, this isn’t the way to do it. The lag is severe for many countries, and the timegated content is unfair — players in some regions have to log in during work hours or in the middle of the night to participate. Event and activity times are only shown in one timezone (UTC-2), instead of displaying the player’s local time or at least including an in-game clock.

[b]Story quality.[/b]
Oh boy — the story is a mess. Streamers claimed it was “better” than the old Blue Protocol story, and I highly disagree. It feels short, lifeless, and rushed, with too many black screens and white text instead of proper animation. The pacing is all over the place, and the grammatical errors are constant. The original story was engaging even though I didn’t understand everything — but this one? No thank you.

[b]Grammatical and translation errors.[/b]
I’m convinced the translation was done by an AI — and not a good one. The amount of grammatical mistakes is overwhelming, and I’m tired of poor translations in games that ask for real money.

[b]Pay-to-win systems.[/b]
The pay-to-win elements are far worse than they were ever presented. The developers even admitted in the CN version that they placed Skill Books in the Auction House directly from the GM side to keep things “in stock.” But the only players who can afford to buy these in bulk are whales. And that’s not the only problem: materials for Imagines can be bought with Bound Rose Orbs, which can be endlessly converted from normal Rose Orbs — because GMs are also putting endless Bound Rose Orbs on the market for conversion. This is unacceptable. Honestly, I would have preferred the rumor about botting over learning that the staff themselves are responsible.

[b]The “give us feedback” situation.[/b]
Since the CBT, APlus has said they wanted player feedback to improve the game. We — the players — gave that feedback, with many posts getting 200+ votes in their Discord section. There was even a dedicated thread for grammatical errors. Yet, to this day, none of this feedback has been properly addressed. No corrections have been made to the reported translation errors, and there has been no acknowledgment of any major player suggestions. I don’t mean that things haven’t been implemented — I mean they haven’t even been discussed. We still don’t know whether any of our feedback is being considered at all.

[b]I’m deeply disappointed in this game.[/b]
As long as the negative points I’ve listed are not properly addressed, I won’t be spending any more time playing it.

[h3]EDIT course to the response from the APlus Team: [/h3]
If you are genuinely committed to resolving these issues, where are the updates and fixes for the translation errors? What is the current status of the ongoing megaserver problems? Up to this point, we have only seen maintenance announcements and new gacha content. The game has been out for nearly a month, and none of the easily addressable issues have been fixed.

review:
This hit me with an unexpected wave of nostalgia. The atmosphere, art style and soundtrack feel like something I've experienced before, turns out, I kinda have. It's got that old soul, reimagined in a smoother, more accessible form. Technically it impressed me. The game ran incredibly smooth on my device with stable FPS, no input delay and good optimzation for a cross-platform title. The combat feels responsive and flashy enough without overdoing it, and loading transition is half-seamless. From a software perspective, I deeply appreciate the engine-side efficiency.

However, I feel like the netcode could use stronger client-side prediction. Menus are also messy as there's too much information stacked on top of itself. Then there's too much currencies (GACHA SLOP) Monetization system feels bloated and unintuitive, like multiple systems were stitched together without unifying logic. Enemies and Bosses also lack behavioural complexity. Once you read their patterns, combat gets repetitive. Music is stunning but environmental sounds and SFX often overpower dialogues. PC performance is above average but mobile still suffers from inconsistent frame pacing and thermal throttling. 

Storywise, it's a mixed bag because it starts strong which feels cinematic, kinda emotional with that classic "you're chosen by fate" tone but it progresses surprisingly fast, skipping over emotional beats that deserved more weight. Then suddenly, it slows down again with long exposition and filler-style quests. It is both draggy and rushed, which sounds weird but fits. Some plot points resolve too quickly, other lingers too long. The world map is beautiful but lacks the depth or substance to make you feel its history. I found myself caring the vibe more than the story itself (pretty, nostalgic but surface-lvl) 

There's a potential here. It just needs tighter pacing and more emotional grounding which I'm looking forward soon.

review:
This free-to-play title delivers a refreshing change of pace. While some progression can feel drawn out, the beautiful art style and satisfying combat make up for it. It’s a decent game overall—so let’s take a closer look.

Graphics: The art style is distinctive and beautifully executed, offering a refreshing visual identity. Combat animations and graphical details across the board are impressive and enjoyable to watch. Unfortunately, the game is capped at 120 FPS. While that’s acceptable for this genre, the difference between 120 and 360 is noticeable—higher frame rates would certainly enhance the experience. Still, it’s a visually striking game overall.

Audio: The sound design is excellent, with strong voice acting and impactful combat audio. Interestingly, while the text can be switched to English, all spoken dialogue and audio remain in the original Asian language, requiring players to rely on subtitles. It’s an unusual localization choice, but not a dealbreaker—overall, the audio experience is impressive.

Controls: It’s straightforward to pick up and play, much like most MMORPGs.

Game-play and everything else after: It’s a free-to-play MMORPG, which sounds great on paper. And yes, you can explore the world with friends, tackle dungeons, and take on some quests together. But I stress some, because there are frustrating moments where certain quests throw you into solo instances, locking your friends out entirely. Why it’s designed this way is anyone’s guess, but it does undermine the whole “play together” vibe. Thankfully, once you’re past the questing phase, the endgame opens up and that’s where group play really shines.

There’s a huge variety of skills and talents to unlock, letting you shape your character however you like. You’re not locked into any one path—there are (I think) nine distinct skill lines, each with its own visuals, mechanics, and roles across assault, defence, and support. You can switch between them freely, which is a big win for flexibility and experimentation.

Now, about XP… brace yourself. Yes, there’s a ton of XP to earn—but it’s a grind, and I say that with emphasis. You’ll see missions boasting “1 million XP in minutes!” but when a single level demands 20 billion, those numbers start to feel absurd. Same goes for currency: you might have 2 million (not called gold, but you get the idea), yet upgrading one item could cost 600K. It’s a game of inflated stats—everything’s big, flashy, and often misleading. That “250 million XP reward” sounds amazing until you realise you need 600 billion to level up. You get the picture.

The map is vast and full of activities—dungeons, trials, raids, bosses (including world bosses), plus farming, mining, alchemy, and more. But remember that XP grind? It applies here too. Levelling up in these side systems takes serious time and effort.

Menus… menus everywhere. Navigation can be a headache. There are layers upon layers of menus, and finding what you need isn’t always intuitive. Thankfully, the game uses orange exclamation marks to flag things you can redeem or check out, which helps a lot. Still, it’s a UI jungle.

Customisation? Deep but confusing. There’s loads of cosmetic and gear customisation, but unlocking certain items can be a puzzle. The currency system is especially messy—four main types, each tied to different mechanics. Some items require real money, others need farming, and some (like Meowlux premium cards) cost 950K each, and you might need 15 or more. It’s a lot to track, and not always well explained.

Expect to spend a fair amount of time running back and forth—but thankfully, the game offers some clever navigation features to ease the journey. Traversal is genuinely enjoyable, with unlockable abilities like mounts, gliding, and dashing layered on top of your standard character skills. These world-based movement options add a nice touch of flair and freedom.

Slightly more playful tone: Yes, there’s a lot of running around—but the game throws in some neat tricks to keep it interesting. Auto-navigation helps, and the traversal abilities—like mounts, gliding, and dashing—add a fun layer on top of your regular skills. It’s a nice mix that makes getting from A to B feel less like a chore.

It’s a fairly enjoyable open-world MMO. The quests are well-designed, missions are plentiful, side content is abundant, and the various runs offer a good dose of fun.

Conversational and casual: It’s a fun open-world MMO—at least to a certain extent. Quests are solid, there’s no shortage of missions, side activities are packed in, and the runs are genuinely entertaining.

Slightly more critical but fair: While not perfect, it’s an enjoyable open-world MMO. The quests hold up well, missions are everywhere, side content is dense, and the runs keep things lively.

Standard gear progression applies—basic gear does the job, but stronger sets offer better stats and performance. You’ll be farming for upgrades, and if you’ve played any MMORPG before, you’ll know exactly what to expect.

Would I recommend the game? Yes, it's a free to play MMORPG with some little differences and nice art style, worth a go at no cost to be fair.
